transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming. Can you tell me what's been bothering you or what brought you in to see me today?

Hi, thank you. Well, I'm a health services manager, and what finally pushed me to come in is... I'm just having a really hard time staying focused at work. Like, I can start working on an EPIC quality report, or I'll sit down in a clinic metrics meeting with every intention of tracking what's going on, and within just a few minutes, my mind has completely drifted. I'll find myself rereading the exact same numbers over and over, or I'll suddenly realize I've missed the entire point of the discussion. It's just getting really frustrating.
Have you struggled with staying focused like this since you were a kid, or is this a change from how you used to be, say within the last few months?

No, it's definitely not a new thing. It's... well, it's been like this since I was a kid, really. Even back in elementary school, I remember teachers writing on my report cards that I was bright but careless. And my mother actually had to sit right there with me while I finished my homework. If she didn't, I would just lose track of my assignments, or we'd realize I completely forgot to bring my books home from school. So, yeah, it's been a lifelong thing, not just the last few months.

latest_inference.note: Lifelong history of inattentive symptoms since childhood (report cards, needing supervision for homework) strongly supports ADHD, predominantly inattentive presentation, and rules out mood/anxiety/adjustment disorders which typically have a defined onset rather than lifelong course.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes a lifelong (since elementary school) pattern of inattentive symptoms—mind wandering during tasks/meetings, rereading material without absorbing it, careless errors noted by teachers, and reliance on external supervision (mother) to complete homework/assignments. These symptoms have persisted into adulthood and now cause clear occupational impairment (difficulty tracking clinic metrics, missing key discussion points at work). No hyperactive or impulsive symptoms were reported, supporting a predominantly inattentive presentation rather than combined or hyperactive-impulsive type.
